description_full: Herbalife Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, provides health and wellness products in North America, Mexico, South and Central America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, China, and the Asia Pacific. It offers weight management products, including meal replacement, protein shakes, drink mixes, weight loss supplements, healthy snacks, and metabolism boosting teas; targeted nutrition products comprising functional beverages and dietary and nutritional supplements containing herbs, vitamins, minerals and other natural ingredients; energy, sports, and fitness products; and facial skin care, body care, and hair care products. The company also provides literature, promotional, and other materials, such as start-up kits, sales tools, and educational materials. It sells its products through sales representatives, independent service providers, and company-operated retail stores and platforms. The company was formerly known as Herbalife Nutrition Ltd. and changed its name to Herbalife Ltd. in April 2023. Herbalife Ltd. was founded in 1980 and is headquartered in Los Angeles, California.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 8K people. Revenue per employee of $593K ranks in the above the sector median among Consumer Defensive peers. Each employee generates $30K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $5K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (9/10).
financial_summary: Herbalife Ltd. is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $1.6B market cap on $5.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 39% against a 9% cost of capital — a 31-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 80% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $253M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.46× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.2× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 5.0% of the shares.

sect: Its 10% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.18x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-8.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 37% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 60% and a beta of 0.82, it moves roughly with the market.
About $18.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 72% in the 2022 bear market and 75% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 76% below its DCF fair value of $62.60, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 5%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $46.18 to $85.23 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 9.0 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 5.1 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 6.3 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 43% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 15.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 14.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $17.33 on average, 13% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 39% clears the cost of capital of 8.7% by 31pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.38).
It runs a 80% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.46x.
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.7x net debt to EBITDA ($353.1M of cash against $2.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.2x.
Working capital ties up about 142 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.1% over 3 years, -1.9% over 5 years and 1.2% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 45% of profits supports about 17.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -13.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 2, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 5.9% on average.
own: Insiders own 5.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 4 sales over the past year, net $2.5M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.5% (0.5% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 0.8% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 8,500 employees, each generates about $593K of revenue, 1.2x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 4.2% a year.
That works out to $30K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
